Senses.Explanation: To chew over is to find material for conceptual working, verbal rumination, or sustained investigation. Chan records extend the bodily action to sayings and public cases: Yunxi Langting Ting tells beginners to “chew over a ready-made sentence that cannot be knocked down” and repeats “chew it over, chew it over” (咬嚼來、咬嚼去); the same record says Wujin spent his whole life unable to chew through “the bowl-carrying public case” (托缽公案). Senses.Explanation: The parent image names verbal entanglement in Chan records, but this exact compound is very thin and occurs only in late framing prose. Gao Shitai's prefatory verse praises the record owner for effacing forms and cutting vine-tangle; a preface says that Linji's staff and shout cut all vine-tangle; a biographical preface pairs cutting vine-tangle with destroying thorn thickets. The Zen deviation comes from the established Chan use of creepers for entangling words, here made the object of cutting. Unlike more common longer forms that add an explicit verb of severing, the exact phrase is not attested by the corpus search as a live-exchange command, so this entry does not present it as one.

Senses.Explanation: Cutting the cat names Nanquan’s canonical action and functions as a later benchmark for decisive conduct. This graph form occurs 278 times in 119 texts and is the orthographic counterpart of “cut the cat” (斬猫), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts the cat in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase functions as case narration and title, an object of questions, a subject for verses, and a cited precedent. One public exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; Miyun Yuanwu tells the questioner to repent. Another sermon quotes the rule to rescue animals from killing and asks how Nanquan's cat and Guizong's snake could have been saved. These passages establish the corpus's own precept relation without stating Nanquan's intention. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers only, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports and rejects students' labels “timely wondrous function” and “great function appears, not retaining rules.”
